entities.summary:
Bárid mac Ímar, a pivotal ninth-century Norse-Gaelic ruler, established himself as King of Dublin and a prominent leader within the Uí Ímair dynasty, a powerful family that dominated much of the Irish Sea region and parts of Scotland and Northumbria during the Viking Age. His reign, culminating in his death in 881 CE, marked a critical period for Viking expansion and consolidation in Ireland, as he navigated complex alliances and fierce rivalries with other Norse chieftains and indigenous Irish kingdoms. As a son of Ímar, one of the legendary 'Kings of the Northmen of all Ireland and Britain,' Bárid inherited a formidable but contested legacy, striving to maintain and expand his family's dominion over strategic maritime territories.

Bárid's early career was characterized by intense conflict, notably his struggle for control of Dublin with Halfdan Ragnarsson, another prominent Uí Ímair member, which resulted in Halfdan's death in 877 CE. Following this consolidation of power, Bárid engaged in extensive military campaigns across the Irish Sea, leading a major expedition to Scotland in 875 CE alongside his kinsman, Óláfr. He was active in raiding and establishing influence in the Hebrides and potentially parts of mainland Scotland, further entrenching Norse presence. In 877 CE, he returned to Northumbria, where he was ambushed and nearly captured by the forces of the Irish king Áed mac Cináeda, demonstrating the constant peril and shifting allegiances of the era.

entities.summary:
Bárid mac Ímar, a pivotal figure in the Uí Ímair dynasty, rose to prominence as King of Dublin during the tumultuous late 9th century, a period marked by intense Viking expansion and consolidation in the Irish Sea region. As a son of Ímar (Ivar Ragnarsson), one of the most formidable Viking leaders, Bárid inherited a legacy of aggressive raiding and strategic settlement. His reign, culminating in his death in 881 CE, was characterized by sustained efforts to establish and defend Norse dominance over key port towns and trade routes, significantly shaping the nascent Hiberno-Norse polities of Ireland and the Isles.

Bárid's early career involved extensive raiding alongside his kinsmen, notably in Scotland, where he participated in the siege of Dumbarton in 870 CE, a major victory that crippled the Kingdom of Strathclyde and secured vast numbers of captives and plunder. By 873 CE, Bárid was firmly established as a ruler in Dublin, succeeding his father. His rule saw the construction of fortifications, the imposition of tribute on surrounding Gaelic territories, and the exploitation of Ireland's rich resources through a network of longphorts. He engaged in numerous naval expeditions, solidifying control over the Isle of Man and extending Uí Ímair influence across the Hebrides, transforming Dublin into the heart of a maritime empire.
